# How to Write a Cover Letter With Any AI Assistant

By the end of this guide you'll have a personalised cover letter draft you can edit and send — even if you've never used an AI assistant before. It's for anyone applying for jobs who'd rather spend their energy choosing which roles to apply for, not staring at a blank page.

## Before you start
- **An AI assistant account.** Any mainstream one will do — ChatGPT, Gemini, Claude, Copilot, Le Chat, DeepSeek or similar. A free plan is enough for this task; paid plans just give you more messages or longer replies.
- **The job ad (or your notes about the role).** Either the full advert copy pasted somewhere, or a few sentences about the role and company. You'll feed it into the assistant in Step 2.
- **A short note about you.** Two or three sentences about your background — your current role, one or two relevant wins, and what you're looking for next. The more honest and specific, the better the draft.
- **Roughly 15 minutes.** That's enough to gather your notes, run the prompt, and do one editing pass.
- **Honest expectation:** the assistant will draft the letter for you. It cannot apply for the job, attach your CV, or speak to the employer on your behalf — those parts are still you.

## Step 1 — Open a fresh conversation in your AI assistant
Open your AI assistant in a browser or app and start a brand-new chat. **What you see:** an empty message box at the bottom of the screen, usually with a placeholder like "Message…" or "Ask anything". **What happens next:** nothing yet — the assistant waits for your first instruction. **If it looks different:** any assistant will do, so if you can't find the "new chat" option, just close the old conversation and open a new tab or window; the next message you send will start fresh. **You'll know it worked when…** you see an empty chat with no previous messages above the input box.

💬 Example: a simple opening instruction — *"I'd like your help drafting a cover letter. I'll give you the job ad and a bit about me — please ask me any clarifying questions first."*

## Step 2 — Paste the job ad and your background into the chat
In that empty message box, paste the job advert (or a summary of it) and then, on the next line, your short note about yourself. **What you see:** the job text followed by a paragraph about you, all sitting in one message. **What happens next:** the assistant reads both pieces together and starts to work out what's relevant. **If it looks different:** if the advert is very long, a short summary is fine — bullet points like "Role: Office Manager. Location: Brisbane. Must have: Xero, scheduling, customer emails" works just as well as full text. **You'll know it worked when…** the assistant replies with at least one clarifying question (e.g. "What's the tone you want — formal or conversational?") instead of jumping straight to a draft.

💬 Example: *"Role: Receptionist at a small accounting firm in Adelaide. Must have: front-desk experience, MYOB or Xero, friendly phone manner. About me: Three years as a receptionist at a dental clinic; comfortable with Xero; looking to move into a professional-services environment. Tone: warm but professional."*

## Step 3 — Ask for a tailored first draft
Once the assistant has asked its questions (or you've answered them in the same message), reply with one clear instruction: write a first draft aimed at this specific role. **What you see:** the assistant begins typing a response in paragraphs — an opener, a middle section about your experience, and a short closing. **What happens next:** a complete draft letter appears, usually in 200–350 words. **If it looks different:** if the draft feels too short or too generic, that's normal — you'll tighten it in Step 4. The first pass is meant to be a starting point, not the final letter. **You'll know it worked when…** there's a full letter on screen with a greeting, body paragraphs, and a sign-off — even if some parts feel a bit "vanilla".

💬 Example: *"Great, thanks. Please now write a first-draft cover letter using the details above. Keep it to about 250 words, three short paragraphs, and don't make up any experience I haven't told you about."*

## Step 4 — Edit the draft to sound like you
Copy the draft into a document (Google Docs, Word, or even the Notes app). Read it aloud once — every awkward phrase will jump out. **What you see:** your draft in an editor where you can freely change words. **What happens next:** you tighten sentences, swap any stiff phrases for words you'd actually say, and cut anything that doesn't match your real experience. **If it looks different:** if a phrase feels too formal for you, shorten it; if a paragraph is empty filler, delete it and replace it with one true sentence about yourself. The assistant wrote it in seconds, so it's fine to rewrite half of it. **You'll know it worked when…** you can read the letter out loud without cringing and every sentence is something you'd genuinely say in an interview.

💬 Example: you might rewrite the closing from *"I look forward to hearing from you at your earliest convenience"* to *"Thanks for reading — I'd love to chat about how I could help your team."*

## Step 5 — Save the prompt that worked so you can reuse it
The exact instruction you used in Step 3 is now a template you can adapt for every other application. **What you see:** your original prompt saved somewhere handy — a notes app, a Google Doc titled "Cover letter prompt", or even an email draft to yourself. **What happens next:** next time you apply somewhere, you change only the role details and the "about me" part, then run the same prompt again. **If it looks different:** if you'd rather not save it digitally, screenshotting the conversation works too. **You'll know it worked when…** the next cover letter takes you roughly five minutes of editing instead of forty minutes of staring at a cursor.

💬 Example: *"Draft a 250-word cover letter for this job: [PASTE NEW JOB AD]. About me: [PASTE NEW ABOUT ME]. Tone: warm but professional."*

## Common mistakes
- **Mistake:** Letting the assistant invent experience you don't have. **Fix:** in Step 3 add a line like *"don't make up any experience I haven't told you about"*. Then delete anything in the draft you can't back up in an interview.
- **Mistake:** Sending the first draft without reading it. **Fix:** always do one slow read aloud in Step 4. Hiring managers can spot an untouched AI letter within a few sentences — usually because the voice doesn't match your emails or the CV attached.
- **Mistake:** Using the same draft for every job. **Fix:** run the prompt again with each new job ad. A personalised paragraph naming the company or role is the single biggest difference between letters that get replies and ones that don't.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** the same prompt-and-edit pattern works for many tricky writing tasks — tenancy letters, school notes, complaint emails, or thank-you notes. Once you've done it once, you've got a reusable skill.
- **For your business or work:** if you help others apply for roles (a small team, a recruitment side hustle, a community group), you can keep a master "about me" paragraph and reuse the same prompt to draft ten letters in an afternoon.
- **If you're just getting started:** pick one real job you'd actually apply for, run Steps 1–4 tonight, and edit the draft until it sounds like you. That's the whole skill, learned in fifteen minutes.

## Try it now
Open your AI assistant right now, paste the job ad for a role you genuinely like, add three sentences about yourself, and ask for a 200-word draft with the instruction *"don't invent any experience I haven't given you"*. You'll have your first usable cover letter before the kettle boils.
